clue.text: Legislator has to look intently at long sentence

parts.note: a life sentence is the longest a court can hand down
to peer is to look closely and intently

explanation.surface: A lawmaker condemned to stare at a prisoner's lengthy sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads as PEER placed at LIFE, so the long sentence comes first. A LIFE PEER is a member of Britain's House of Lords whose title is not inherited.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the House of Lords, including those appointed for their lifetime, help make British law, so they count as lawmakers.

clue.text: Business graduate in final thrash

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped by the outer piece

parts.note: the final one is the last
a Master of Business Administration holds an MBA

explanation.surface: A business-school graduate taking part in a deciding contest, perhaps a beating in the last round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Final thrash' sounds like an end-of-term party, but 'thrash' is the definition and 'final' is wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To lambast someone is to beat or attack them severely, a synonym of thrash in both its physical and verbal senses.

clue.text: Having plenty of money, not proud

definitions.meaning: first meaning: well supplied with cash
second meaning: level with a surface, not sticking out from it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Proud' here is the carpenter's sense of projecting above a surface, so 'not proud' means level, not humble.
explanation.definitionFit: Flush describes someone temporarily rich and also a surface exactly level with its neighbour, with nothing protruding.

clue.text: Partial sense spoiled polite remarks

indicators.note: something spoiled has been ruined and knocked out of its proper shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, twelve letters of fodder

explanation.surface: Half-hearted compliments that are spoilt by only partly making sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partial' looks like a description of the sense, but the two words together are just the letters to be mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasantries are the small courteous exchanges of conversation, such as greetings and small talk, which are polite remarks.

clue.text: Consumed portion of meat enchilada

indicators.note: a portion is just a part of a whole, so a run of letters is taken from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone has wolfed down a serving of a meat-filled Mexican tortilla.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across the two words of the dish, starting inside 'meat'.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that has been consumed has been eaten, both past participles describing a meal finished off.

clue.text: Anti-American slogan shows common sense

indicators.note: a slogan is a short chanted phrase, so the pieces are read together as words someone might shout

parts.note: being against something is saying no to it
the United States, abbreviated

explanation.surface: Protesters chanting against America are said to be showing good sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The slogan is the two words NO and US run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Nous is a British informal word, borrowed from Greek for mind, meaning practical intelligence or good judgement.

clue.text: Taking breakfast, say, love to start with porridge

indicators.note: something placed to start with goes at the front, ahead of the other piece

parts.note: love is a zero score in tennis, shaped like the letter O
someone taking breakfast is at a meal; 'say' marks breakfast as one example

explanation.surface: Someone eating breakfast, with a loving touch, begins with a bowl of porridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love' gives O by the tennis-score convention, and it is placed before AT MEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal is the North American name for porridge made from ground or rolled oats cooked in water or milk.

clue.text: Engineer traps young herring

indicators.note: to engineer something is to construct or contrive it, so these letters are rebuilt into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An engineer has built a contraption that catches small fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like the person doing the trapping, but it is a verb telling you to rebuild the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprat is a small fish of the herring family, and the name is also used loosely for juvenile herring.

clue.text: Argument: lash out, and that could mean prison

definitions.text: Argument: lash out, and that could mean prison

indicators.note: out can mean wild or wrong, so the preceding letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A row turns violent, and the person who hits out may end up behind bars.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a quarrel where someone lashes out and kills is the crime that sends them to prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Manslaughter is unlawful killing without intent to murder, the typical charge when a heated quarrel ends in a fatal blow and a jail term.

clue.text: Doctor to take advantage of computer equipment

parts.note: MO is Medical Officer, a military doctor
to use someone is to take advantage of them

explanation.surface: A physician exploiting the office computer kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take advantage of' looks like one phrase, but 'of' is the link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mouse is the hand-held pointing device that sits beside a keyboard, a standard piece of computer hardware.

clue.text: One checking for poison impounds old kitchen appliance

indicators.note: to impound is to shut something away in an enclosure, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: a food taster samples a ruler's meals to check for poison
O is a standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A royal food-taster confiscates an antique kitchen gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old kitchen appliance' reads as one phrase, but 'old' belongs to the wordplay and only 'kitchen appliance' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A toaster is the electric device that browns slices of bread, a fixture on most kitchen worktops.

clue.text: Tree has to evolve

indicators.note: to evolve is to change form gradually, so these letters change into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tree is obliged to develop over time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has to' looks like one verb phrase meaning must, but 'has' is the fodder and 'to' merely links it to its indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The ash is a common deciduous tree with winged seeds and pale tough timber, a specific example of a tree.

clue.text: Showing signs of age, mangling sentences

indicators.note: mangling something crushes it out of shape, so these letters come out in a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly speaker whose grammar is starting to fall apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole opening phrase, an adjective just like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Senescent is the formal word for growing old and deteriorating, from the Latin for becoming elderly.

clue.text: Speaker's disconcerted in high seat

indicators.note: a speaker says words out loud, so the word is judged by how it sounds rather than how it is written

parts.note: someone disconcerted is thrown, put off their stride

explanation.surface: The Speaker of a parliament is flustered while sitting in an elevated chair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speaker' suggests the parliamentary Speaker in his chair, but here it means the word is spoken; 'Speaker's' is 'Speaker is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A throne is the raised ceremonial chair of a monarch or bishop, an elevated seat of state.

clue.text: Being fatter, cut game short

indicators.note: something cut short loses its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a British bat-and-ball game, a playground cousin of baseball

explanation.surface: Someone putting on weight has to curtail the match.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the final S of the game is removed. 'Being fatter' is descriptive, as the comparative adjective is.
explanation.definitionFit: Rounder is the comparative of round, and a plumper body is more rounded, so it describes a person who is heavier.

clue.text: One being milked, everyone admitted, is immature

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a dairy cow is milked
everyone is all

explanation.surface: A victim of exploitation, with everyone allowed in on it, behaves childishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being milked' suggests a person being exploited, but it is literal: the animal on the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Callow describes a young person lacking experience and sophistication, so it is a close synonym of immature.

clue.text: Attractive, so have a few successes

parts.note: to have successes is to win; the noun at the end completes this verb
a few is some

explanation.surface: Being good-looking, you'd expect a few victories.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a reworded 'win some', as in 'you win some, you lose some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Winsome means charming and appealing in an innocent way, a synonym of attractive.

clue.text: Level stage in position in field

parts.note: two sides that are level or even are square
a stage of a journey or race is a leg

explanation.surface: A flat platform set up somewhere in a meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: SQUARE LEG is a fielding position in cricket, level with the batsman on the leg side; 'field' is the cricket field, not a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket each fielder stands at a named spot, and square leg is one of those standard placings.

clue.text: Grasslike plant in small border

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a border is an edge

explanation.surface: A grassy plant growing in a narrow garden border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but it only links definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedges are rush-like plants of wet ground with triangular stems, closely resembling grasses.

clue.text: Film solicitor getting divorced from wife

indicators.note: divorce is a separation, so one letter is split off from the rest and dropped

parts.note: a solicitor is a kind of lawyer
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A movie about a divorce lawyer splitting from his wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' wants to be a movie; it is a thin coating. A solicitor is the British name for a lawyer who handles legal paperwork.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin film of oil or dust is a layer, both words describing a sheet of material spread over a surface.

clue.text: Youngster's short aria

indicators.note: something short is lacking a bit at the end, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: an aria is a song in an opera

explanation.surface: A child singing a brief solo.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S stands for 'is', joining the definition to the wordplay rather than marking possession.
explanation.definitionFit: A son is a male child, and a young boy is a common example of a youngster.

clue.text: A little holly perhaps essential to grasp right

indicators.note: what is essential to something lies at its heart, so the letters come from within the following words

parts.note: the letters straddle the gap between the two words

explanation.surface: A small piece of holly, presumably needed to hold the right way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks holly as one example of a plant a small shoot might come from.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig is a small stem bearing leaves, such as the bit of holly placed on a Christmas pudding.

clue.text: Decrepit stranger needs to fill empty diary

indicators.note: to fill something is to go inside it, so one piece sits within another
an empty container has its contents gone, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
stranger means more odd

explanation.surface: A frail old stranger needs something to fill a blank appointment book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stranger' looks like a noun for an unknown person, but it is the comparative adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Doddery means shaky and unsteady through old age, so it is a close synonym of feeble and worn out.

clue.text: Trunk finally sent to Bristol regularly

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the run

explanation.surface: A trunk of luggage eventually dispatched to Bristol on a routine basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To' is part of the fodder, not a link word. Bristol is a city in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk of the body is the torso, the main part without the head, arms and legs.

clue.text: Time to arrest unknown Biblical figure

indicators.note: to arrest is to seize and hold, so one piece holds another inside it

parts.note: an era is a period of time
in algebra unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: The moment has come to detain a mysterious figure from scripture.
explanation.walkthrough: Using Z for an unknown quantity is a borrowing from algebra.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra is the Jewish scribe and priest who gives his name to a book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: Discontinue meetings involving professional rascal

parts.note: short for professional
a rascal is a rogue

explanation.surface: Call off the gatherings that involve a seasoned scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involving' looks like a container signal, but the two pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue a parliament is to suspend its sittings without formally dissolving it, a technical term in Westminster-style government.
